rationale: The supplied evidence (Ezek 31:9 read through the established tree=nation/people pattern of Dan 4, Ezek 17/31, etc.) directly yields the entry's identification: a garden is a planted stand of such trees, i.e., nations/peoples grouped under the divine gardener who plants, envies, fells and raises them. The traditional paradise reading of the same verse is weaker because it leaves the surrounding tree-nation equations and the Isaiah garden texts unexplained, whereas the entry accounts for them without remainder. No material claim printed in the entry itself is left unsupported.
book_core_identification: A garden is a planted grouping of trees, and those trees are nations or peoples arranged together under a gardener's rule.
chapter_only_objections: Isaiah's 'gardens' exclusively mean foreign nations rather than literal cultic groves
the clean/unclean food laws remain eternally binding as the ground of final judgment
the supplied 'tree' in Isa 66:17 is purely translational and the verse means 'following one nation'
strongest_counter_interpretation: In Ezek 31:9 the 'garden of God' is simply Edenic paradise (the archetypal place of divine presence and perfection); the 'trees of Eden' are either literal ideal trees or a local poetic metaphor for other great kingdoms that envy Assyria/Pharaoh, without turning 'garden' itself into a technical term for a grouping of nation-trees.
counter_core_identification: Garden = Edenic paradise, the place of God's presence and original/eschatological perfection.
material_core_denial: The garden is not a planted grouping of nation-trees under a gardener; it is the paradise sanctuary itself.
counter_case: Ezek 31 explicitly places the trees 'in the garden of God' and calls them 'trees of Eden,' language that everywhere else denotes the primal paradise.
The envy motif is a standard hyperbolic comparison of imperial greatness, not a definition of garden as forest-of-nations.
The broader biblical garden pattern (Gen 2–3, Isa 51:3, Ezek 36:35, Rev 22) consistently evokes restored paradise, not political federations.
book_explanatory_advantages: Uniformly extends the already-decoded tree=nation/king equation (Dan 4; Ezek 17; 31) so that a planted collection of trees is simply the corresponding collection of nations.
Makes the divine 'gardener' actions (planting, felling, exalting) in the same chapters literal rather than mixed metaphor.
Supplies a single coherent reading for the Isaiah garden indictments without invoking unstated cult objects.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Preserves the surface Eden/paradise diction of Ezek 31:8–9, 18 without additional symbolic steps.
Aligns with the dominant canonical arc from Genesis garden to Revelation garden-city.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 17:22–24 (trees of the field = nations under the divine gardener)
Chapter's cumulative tree-nation pattern (Assyria cedar, Israel vine/olive/fig, etc.)
